lead: A catalogue lists dozens of bearings that share the same bore, so the designer needs one number that says which of them can do the job. That number is the required basic dynamic load rating C_req. You find the equivalent load from the radial and axial forces, fix the life wanted in hours, convert that life into million revolutions, and compute C_req. Then you pick the smallest bearing whose catalogue rating C is at least C_req, and you check static safety and the limiting speed. Pumps, fans, gearboxes, electric motors and machine tool spindles are all chosen this way.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.6 for C, P and the L10 life equation, and Chapter 5.2 for the rolling bearing types.

sections.h3: Selection means turning load and life into one number

blocks.text: A rolling bearing is not designed from a blank page; it is chosen from a catalogue. For each bearing the catalogue gives a basic dynamic load rating C: the steady load, in newtons, that would give a rating life of one million revolutions. The machine gives you a load and a life in hours. Selection is the step that turns those two into a single number you can compare with the catalogue.
The life equation of Chapter 5.6 links C, P and life. Inverting it gives the rating you must ask the catalogue for.

blocks.where: C_req is the required basic dynamic load rating in N; P is the equivalent dynamic load in N; L10 is the rating life in million revolutions; p = 3 for ball bearings and p = 10/3 for roller bearings.

blocks.text: The life hidden inside C is counted in million revolutions, so the hours must be converted before they enter the formula.

blocks.where: n is the speed in rev/min; L10h is the required life in hours; 60 changes rev/min into rev per hour and 10⁶ changes revolutions into millions; L10 is in million revolutions.

blocks.text: Choose the smallest bearing in the size range whose C is at least C_req. A larger C costs more, weighs more and needs a bigger housing, so an oversized bearing is wasted money. The rating is not the only test, though: the static rating and the limiting speed are checked as well.

Bearings are rated for one kind of load: pure radial, steady, applied through the centre. A real bearing carries a radial load F_r and often an axial load F_a. P is the single radial load that would wear the bearing out in the same number of revolutions as the real combination.

blocks.where: F_r is the radial load in N; F_a is the axial load in N; X is the radial factor and Y the axial factor, both read from the catalogue table for that bearing; P is in N.

blocks.text: The factor e is a threshold fixed by the maker for each bearing, and it depends on how much thrust the bearing already carries compared with C0. Below the threshold the axial load is too small to change the stress field much, so it is dropped and P = F_r. Above it the load zone shifts, more of the rolling element is loaded, and Y grows with F_a/C0.

sections.h3: Static check, speed check, and the order of work

blocks.text: A bearing that turns very slowly, stands still, or takes a heavy shock can fail with no fatigue at all. The rolling elements press dents into the race, called brinelling, and the bearing runs rough for the rest of its life. Against this the catalogue gives a basic static load rating C0, the load at which a fixed small permanent deformation appears.
P0 = F_r   or   P0 = 0.6 × F_r + 0.5 × F_a, whichever is greater
blocks.where: P0 is the equivalent static load in N; the second form applies to radial ball and roller bearings that also carry thrust.

blocks.text: The static safety factor is s0 = C0 ÷ P0. Use about 1.5 to 2 for smooth, quiet running, 2 to 3 for ordinary machinery, and 3 or more where shock is expected. Every catalogue entry also carries a limiting speed, lower for grease and higher for oil; running above it heats the bearing faster than the housing can shed heat.

items: Find F_r and F_a on the bearing from the shaft loads (see Unit 3, Shafts, Keys and Couplings).
Choose a trial bearing type for the duty.
Read e, X and Y from the catalogue for that bearing.
Compute P = X F_r + Y F_a.
Fix the required life L10h and convert it to L10 in million revolutions.
Pick a bearing with C ≥ C_req and the bore the shaft needs.
Check C0/P0 against the static safety factor, and check the limiting speed.

spec.title: Bearing selection
spec.aria: A flow from the radial and axial loads to the equivalent load, the required life, the required dynamic rating, the catalogue choice and the static and speed checks.

examples.question: A deep-groove ball bearing carries a radial load F_r = 5 kN and an axial load F_a = 2 kN at n = 1200 rev/min. The catalogue gives e = 0.28, X = 0.56 and Y = 1.5 for this bearing. The required life is L10h = 10 000 h. Find the equivalent dynamic load, the life in million revolutions, the required basic dynamic load rating, and the equivalent static load for ordinary duty.
steps: Check the ratio: F_a/F_r = 2000/5000 = 0.4 > 0.28 = e, so X = 0.56 and Y = 1.5 apply.
Equivalent dynamic load: P = X F_r + Y F_a = 0.56 × 5000 + 1.5 × 2000 = 2800 + 3000 = 5800 N.
Life in million revolutions: L10 = 60 n L10h / 10⁶ = 60 × 1200 × 10 000 / 10⁶ = 720 million revolutions.
Choose a catalogue bearing in the right bore with C ≥ 52 kN.
With s0 = 2 for ordinary running, C0 must be at least 2 × 5000 = 10 000 N, and the limiting speed must exceed 1200 rev/min.
examples.answer: P = 5800 N, L10 = 720 million revolutions, C_req = 51 984.3 N ≈ 52 kN; the chosen bearing needs C ≥ 52 kN, C0 ≥ 10 kN and a limiting speed above 1200 rev/min.
examples.check:
Fr = 5000.0
Fa = 2000.0
n = 1200.0
L10h = 10000.0
X, Y, p = 0.56, 1.5, 3.0
P = X * Fr + Y * Fa
L10 = 60.0 * n * L10h / 1e6
C_req = P * L10 ** (1.0 / p)
P0 = max(Fr, 0.6 * Fr + 0.5 * Fa)
C0_min = 2.0 * P0
print(round(P, 1))
print(round(L10, 1))
print(round(C_req, 1))
print(round(P0, 1))
print(round(C0_min, 1))

traps: Putting L10h straight into C = P L^(1/3). The life inside the rating is in million revolutions, so 10 000 h at 1200 rev/min becomes 720, not 10 000.
Using Y when F_a/F_r ≤ e. Below the threshold Y = 0 and X = 1, so the axial load drops out; adding Y F_a anyway inflates P and over-sizes the bearing.
Skipping the static check. A shock-loaded or slowly turning bearing can brinell its races even when C ≥ C_req, so compare C0 with P0 and use the static safety factor.
Taking p = 3 for a roller bearing. It is 10/3, and the same P and L10 then give a smaller C_req than a ball bearing would.
Mixing N and kN in P, or forgetting the 60 in the hours-to-revolutions conversion; both give a wrong C_req by a factor that looks plausible on the page.

quiz.q: What does the basic dynamic load rating C of a bearing mean?
quiz.a: The steady load in newtons that gives a rating life of one million revolutions; the catalogue lists it for every bearing.

quiz.q: State the equivalent static load for a radial ball bearing carrying thrust.
quiz.a: P0 is the greater of F_r and 0.6 F_r + 0.5 F_a.

quiz.q: Why must L10h be converted to million revolutions before C_req is computed?
quiz.a: C is defined for a life of one million revolutions, so the life in the rating equation must be in that unit. Using 10 000 h in place of 720 million rev gives 10 000^(1/3) ≈ 21.5 instead of 8.96, so C_req comes out about 2.4 times too large and the bearing is badly over-sized.

quiz.q: Why does the axial load stop mattering below the ratio e?
quiz.a: Below e the thrust is small compared with the bearing's static capacity, the load zone hardly changes, and life is set by the radial load alone. So Y = 0 and P = F_r.

quiz.q: A ball bearing carries F_r = 4 kN and no thrust at n = 900 rev/min, with a required life of 20 000 h. Find C_req.
A roller bearing has P = 6 kN and a required life of 500 million revolutions. Find C_req.
A bearing chosen on the dynamic rating fails within weeks, and its races show brinelling. What was missed?
quiz.a: The static check. Slow, stationary or shock loading dents the races even when C ≥ C_req, so C0/P0 must reach the static safety factor. The limiting speed, misalignment and fits are the other suspects.

beyond: Not for the exam. Standard L10 gives 90% reliability; for higher reliability an adjustment factor a1 below 1 multiplies the life, so the same bearing must be bigger. Modified rating life standards go further and correct C for oil film thickness, contamination and the fatigue load limit of the steel. In industry, bearing firms offer selection software and vibration-based condition monitoring that replaces a fixed life estimate with measured wear. Search for modified rating life, reliability adjustment factor, and bearing vibration signature analysis.
